tagline: Build the medication, safety, and processing knowledge to pass the PTCE.

domains.name: Medications
domains.description: Drug names, classifications, interactions, dosing, storage, and stability.

domains.name: Patient Safety and Quality Assurance
domains.description: Error prevention, high-alert drugs, infection control, and event reporting.

domains.name: Order Entry and Processing
domains.description: Calculations, equipment, NDC/lot/expiration, and returns processing.

domains.name: Federal Requirements
domains.description: Controlled substances, DEA schedules, REMS, recalls, and DSCSA.

questions.stem: A prescription is written for Lipitor. Which generic drug is being dispensed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Lipitor is the brand name for atorvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) used to lower cholesterol. Why the others are wrong: **A** simvastatin is the statin sold as Zocor, a different product; **C** lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor (Prinivil/Zestril) for blood pressure, not a statin; **D** metformin is a biguanide antidiabetic (Glucophage).

questions.stem: Amoxicillin belongs to which class of medications?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, a member of the penicillin (beta-lactam) class of antibiotics. Why the others are wrong: **A** macrolides include azithromycin and erythromycin; **C** fluoroquinolones include ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin; **D** proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole reduce stomach acid and are not antibiotics.

questions.stem: A patient taking warfarin should be monitored for an interaction with which of the following because of an additive risk of bleeding?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Aspirin inhibits platelets and, combined with the anticoagulant warfarin, substantially increases bleeding risk, so this combination warrants pharmacist review. Why the others are wrong: **A** occasional low-dose acetaminophen is generally the preferred analgesic for warfarin patients; **C** calcium carbonate is an antacid/supplement with no major bleeding interaction; **D** loratadine is a non-sedating antihistamine without a significant warfarin interaction.

questions.stem: A nitroglycerin product is ordered to be given SL. By which route should it be administered?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The abbreviation SL means sublingual, meaning the tablet is placed under the tongue to dissolve and absorb through the oral mucosa. Why the others are wrong: **A** intramuscular is abbreviated IM; **B** subcutaneous is abbreviated SC/SubQ; **D** rectal is abbreviated PR. Each of these is a different route from SL.

questions.stem: Which medication is most appropriately stored in the refrigerator (2–8°C) to maintain stability before it is dispensed or opened?

options.text: Amoxicillin oral suspension after it has been reconstituted

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Reconstituted amoxicillin oral suspension is unstable at room temperature and is labeled to be refrigerated, typically discarded after about 14 days. Why the others are wrong: **B**, **C**, and **D** are solid oral tablets that are stored at controlled room temperature, not refrigerated.

questions.stem: Metoprolol is classified as which type of cardiovascular agent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Metoprolol is a beta-adrenergic blocker (beta blocker), recognizable by the -olol stem, used for hypertension and heart conditions. Why the others are wrong: **A** loop diuretics include furosemide; **B** ACE inhibitors end in -pril (e.g., lisinopril); **C** calcium channel blockers include amlodipine and diltiazem.

questions.stem: A patient is already taking lisinopril for blood pressure. A prescriber sends a new prescription for benazepril. Why should this be flagged for the pharmacist?

options.text: The two drugs are in completely unrelated classes with no concern
It is a therapeutic duplication—both are ACE inhibitors
Benazepril is a beta blocker that should not follow an ACE inhibitor
Lisinopril must always be taken with a second ACE inhibitor

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Lisinopril and benazepril are both ACE inhibitors, so prescribing them together is a therapeutic duplication that the pharmacist should review. Why the others are wrong: **A** the drugs are in the same class, so there is a concern; **C** benazepril is an ACE inhibitor, not a beta blocker; **D** patients are not given two ACE inhibitors at once.

questions.stem: Which two of the following correctly pair a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) generic drug with its brand name? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Omeprazole is sold as Prilosec and pantoprazole as Protonix; both are PPIs with the -prazole stem. Why the others are wrong: **C** famotidine is an H2 blocker (Pepcid), not Prilosec; **D** esomeprazole's brand is Nexium, whereas Zantac was ranitidine (an H2 blocker).

questions.stem: A common side effect that the labeling for diphenhydramine (Benadryl) warns about is:
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Diphenhydramine is a first-generation (sedating) antihistamine, so drowsiness is a hallmark side effect and the basis for its "may cause marked drowsiness" warning. Why the others are wrong: **A** hair loss is not a typical antihistamine effect; **B** anticholinergics tend to cause urinary retention, not increased urination; **D** a dry cough is associated with ACE inhibitors, not antihistamines.

questions.stem: Insulin glargine (Lantus) that is unopened and being stored as backup stock should be kept:

options.text: In direct sunlight to keep it warm
In the freezer to extend its shelf life
On the shelf at room temperature indefinitely
In the refrigerator until its expiration date

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Unopened insulin is stored refrigerated (2–8°C) until the labeled expiration date; once in use it may be kept at room temperature for a limited period. Why the others are wrong: **A** heat and direct light degrade insulin; **B** insulin must never be frozen, which destroys it; **C** unopened insulin is not stored at room temperature indefinitely.

questions.stem: Omeprazole (Prilosec) reduces stomach acid by acting as which type of agent?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor, recognizable by the -prazole stem, that blocks the gastric H+/K+ ATPase pump. Why the others are wrong: **B** H2 blockers end in -tidine (e.g., famotidine); **C** antacids such as calcium carbonate neutralize existing acid rather than blocking its production; **D** omeprazole is not an antibiotic.

questions.stem: A patient taking the MAO inhibitor phenelzine asks the pharmacy about taking an OTC decongestant containing pseudoephedrine. Why does this combination require pharmacist intervention?

options.text: It has no meaningful interaction and is always safe
It can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure (hypertensive crisis)
It causes the decongestant to lose all effectiveness
It turns the urine bright orange

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Combining an MAO inhibitor with a sympathomimetic such as pseudoephedrine can trigger a hypertensive crisis, a serious interaction the pharmacist must address. Why the others are wrong: **A** there is a serious interaction, so it is not always safe; **C** the issue is excessive sympathetic effect, not loss of effect; **D** orange urine is associated with phenazopyridine, not this combination.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are correctly paired generic-and-brand combinations? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Metformin is sold as Glucophage and furosemide is sold as Lasix; both pairings are correct. Why the others are wrong: **C** Coumadin is warfarin, not hydrochlorothiazide (brand Microzide); **D** Synthroid is levothyroxine, while albuterol's brands include ProAir and Ventolin.

questions.stem: Which two medications are commonly available as inhaled dosage forms for respiratory conditions? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Albuterol (a short-acting bronchodilator) and fluticasone (an inhaled corticosteroid) are both delivered by inhalation for asthma and COPD. Why the others are wrong: **C** metoprolol is an oral beta blocker for cardiovascular use; **D** omeprazole is an oral/IV proton pump inhibitor, not an inhaled product.

questions.stem: A patient on simvastatin presents a new prescription for clarithromycin. Why should the pharmacist be alerted to this combination?

options.text: They must always be taken together for the statin to work
The two drugs cancel each other out and both become ineffective
Clarithromycin inhibits the metabolism of simvastatin, raising the risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis
The combination is preferred and needs no review

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor that raises simvastatin levels, increasing the risk of muscle toxicity (myopathy and rhabdomyolysis), so the combination warrants pharmacist review. Why the others are wrong: **A** the drugs are not required to be co-administered; **B** the concern is increased statin exposure, not loss of effect; **D** the interaction is harmful, so review is needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is classified by ISMP as a high-alert medication because errors carry a heightened risk of significant patient harm?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Insulin is a classic high-alert medication; dosing errors can cause severe hypoglycemia, so extra safeguards are used. Why the others are wrong: **B** standard acetaminophen tablets, **C** loratadine, and **D** docusate are low-risk agents not on the high-alert list.

questions.stem: Writing the drug name as "hydrOXYzine" and "hydrALAZINE" is an example of which error-prevention strategy?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Tall Man lettering uses mixed-case letters to highlight the differing parts of look-alike/sound-alike names, helping distinguish hydrOXYzine from hydrALAZINE. Why the others are wrong: **A** the 'rights' are a checklist for safe administration, not a naming convention; **B** a leading zero is for decimal numbers (0.5 mg); **C** bar-code scanning verifies products electronically.

questions.stem: A patient drops off a prescription and mentions a new symptom that may be an allergic reaction to a current medication. What is the most appropriate action for the pharmacy technician?

options.text: Refer the patient to the pharmacist for counseling and clinical assessment
Advise the patient to stop all medications immediately
Recommend an antihistamine dose to treat the reaction
Tell the patient the symptom is unrelated and dispense as written

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Clinical judgment, counseling, and assessing a possible adverse reaction are the pharmacist's responsibility, so the technician refers the patient. Why the others are wrong: **B**, **C**, and **D** all require clinical decisions—stopping therapy, recommending treatment, or judging causality—that are outside the technician's scope.

questions.stem: A patient experiences a serious, unexpected side effect from a prescription drug. Which program is the FDA's system for voluntarily reporting such adverse events?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** MedWatch is the FDA's program for reporting adverse events and product problems associated with drugs and medical devices. Why the others are wrong: **A** VAERS is specifically for vaccine adverse events; **C** a PDMP is a prescription drug monitoring program for controlled substances; **D** REMS is a risk management strategy, not an adverse-event reporting system.

questions.stem: An adverse event following administration of a vaccine should be reported to which surveillance program?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** VAERS, co-managed by the CDC and FDA, is the national system for reporting adverse events after vaccination. Why the others are wrong: **A** a MedGuide is FDA-approved patient information, not a reporting system; **B** MedWatch covers drugs and devices generally; **D** DSCSA is the supply-chain track-and-trace law.

questions.stem: During order entry, which two findings should a technician flag for the pharmacist to review rather than resolve independently? (Select two.)

options.text: A drug utilization review (DUR) alert for a major drug-drug interaction
A potential allergy between the new drug and an allergy listed in the patient's profile
A patient asking for the pharmacy's hours
A label that needs more printer paper loaded

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A DUR interaction alert and a possible drug-allergy conflict both require the pharmacist's clinical judgment, so the technician must refer them. Why the others are wrong: **C** giving store hours is general information a technician can handle; **D** loading printer paper is a routine operational task, not a clinical issue.

questions.stem: After a significant medication error, a pharmacy convenes a team to identify the underlying system causes rather than to assign individual blame. This structured analysis is called:
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Root cause analysis is a systematic, non-punitive review of why an error occurred so process improvements can prevent recurrence. Why the others are wrong: **A** inventory turnover analysis is a financial/stock metric; **B** a DUR evaluates prescribing/therapy appropriateness; **C** a formulary review decides which drugs are stocked or covered.

questions.stem: Which two practices help prevent dispensing errors caused by look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) medications? (Select two.)

options.text: Using Tall Man lettering on labels and shelf tags
Storing LASA products in separated locations or with shelf alerts
Removing all bar codes to speed up dispensing
Using only trailing zeros on every dose (e.g., 5.0 mg)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Tall Man lettering and physically separating or flagging look-alike products both reduce mix-ups between similar drug names. Why the others are wrong: **C** bar codes are a key verification safeguard and should not be removed; **D** trailing zeros (5.0 mg) cause tenfold dosing errors and are prohibited.

questions.stem: Before compounding sterile preparations, performing proper hand hygiene and donning appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) primarily serves to:

options.text: Prevent contamination and reduce the risk of infection
Improve the taste of the final product
Eliminate the need for a laminar airflow hood

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Hand hygiene and PPE are core infection-prevention measures that protect the preparation and personnel from contamination. Why the others are wrong: **B** the goal is safety, not speed; **C** taste is irrelevant to sterile compounding; **D** PPE does not replace the primary engineering control (the laminar airflow hood).

questions.stem: Place the following PPE items in the correct order in which they are donned before entering a cleanroom buffer area for sterile compounding, from first to last.

options.text: Shoe covers, then head/facial hair cover and face mask
Perform hand hygiene (wash hands and forearms)
Sterile gloves (after hand antisepsis inside the buffer area)

questions.explanation: Garbing for sterile compounding proceeds from the dirtiest to the cleanest activities. You first don shoe covers, then the head and facial-hair covers and face mask while still in the ante-area (A); next you perform thorough hand and forearm hygiene (B); then you put on the non-shedding gown (C); and finally, after hand antisepsis, you don sterile gloves (D) as the last step before working in the hood. This sequence keeps the most critical barrier—sterile gloves—applied last so it stays clean.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs is a well-known look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drug name combination?

options.text: Insulin and heparin given by the same route

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Celebrex (celecoxib) and Celexa (citalopram) are a classic LASA pair whose similar spelling and sound cause mix-ups. Why the others are wrong: **A** aspirin and ibuprofen are both NSAIDs but their names are not confusable; **C** insulin and heparin are both high-alert drugs but are not name look-alikes; **D** calcium and potassium are distinct electrolytes, not a LASA name pair.

questions.stem: Place the following steps of processing a new retail prescription in the correct order, from first to last.

options.text: Receive the prescription and confirm patient and insurance information
Enter the prescription into the system (drug, directions, quantity)
Pharmacist performs the final verification before the drug is dispensed

questions.explanation: A prescription moves through a fixed workflow: first it is received and the patient/insurance details are confirmed (A); next the technician enters the order into the system (B); then the medication is filled and labeled (C); and finally the pharmacist performs the final clinical verification before the product is dispensed (D). The pharmacist's check is always last because the technician may prepare but cannot verify the final product.

questions.stem: A patient weighs 154 lb. What is the patient's weight in kilograms (round to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** 1 kg = 2.2 lb, so 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg. Why the others are wrong: **A** multiplies by 2.2 instead of dividing; **B** leaves the value in pounds without converting; **D** results from dividing by 2 rather than 2.2.

questions.stem: A prescription is for amoxicillin 500 mg capsules, 1 capsule three times daily for 10 days. How many capsules should be dispensed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Three times daily equals 3 capsules per day, and 3 × 10 days = 30 capsules. Why the others are wrong: **A** is unrelated to the math (3 × 10); **B** counts only one day's supply; **C** assumes twice daily.

questions.stem: A 150 mL bottle of cough syrup is dispensed with directions to take 10 mL three times daily. What is the days supply?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The patient uses 10 mL × 3 = 30 mL per day, so 150 mL ÷ 30 mL/day = 5 days. Why the others are wrong: **A** divides 150 by 10 (ignores the three doses); **C** uses 15 mL/day; **D** does not reflect the calculation.

questions.stem: How many milliliters of a 1:1000 epinephrine solution contain 0.5 mg of epinephrine?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A 1:1000 solution is 1 g per 1000 mL, i.e., 1 mg/mL, so 0.5 mg occupies 0.5 mL. Why the others are wrong: **A** is off by a factor of ten; **B** would be 5 mg at 1 mg/mL; **D** would contain 1 mg, not 0.5 mg.

questions.stem: Using alligation, how many parts of a 70% dextrose solution and a 5% dextrose solution are needed to prepare a 10% dextrose solution?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** By alligation, the parts of 70% equal the difference 10 − 5 = 5, and the parts of 5% equal 70 − 10 = 60, giving 5 parts of 70% to 60 parts of 5%. Why the others are wrong: **A** equal parts would yield a 37.5% solution, far above the target; **B** reverses the proportions; **C** uses incorrect differences.

questions.stem: An IV is ordered to infuse 1000 mL over 8 hours using tubing with a drop factor of 15 gtt/mL. What is the flow rate in drops per minute (round to the nearest whole number)?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** 1000 mL ÷ 480 min = 2.08 mL/min; multiplied by 15 gtt/mL ≈ 31 gtt/min. Why the others are wrong: **B** 125 mL/hr is the volumetric rate, not gtt/min; **C** simply restates the drop factor; **D** does not follow from the calculation.

questions.stem: On a National Drug Code (NDC) number, what does the middle segment identify?

options.text: The specific product: strength, dosage form, and formulation
The pharmacy that dispensed the drug

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An NDC has three segments—labeler, product, and package; the middle (product) segment identifies the strength, dosage form, and formulation. Why the others are wrong: **A** the labeler/manufacturer is the first segment; **C** package size is the third segment; **D** the dispensing pharmacy is not encoded in the NDC.

questions.stem: A product is labeled with an expiration date of '08/2026' and no specific day. According to standard practice, through what date is it considered usable?

options.text: Through the last day of August 2026 (08/31/2026)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When only a month and year are given, the product is usable through the last day of that month, so 08/2026 means it expires after August 31, 2026. Why the others are wrong: **B** and **C** end the date too early within the month; **D** uses the prior month entirely.

questions.stem: Which two items of information are encoded by a manufacturer's lot number and expiration date on a stock bottle? (Select two.)

options.text: The specific production batch (for recall tracing)
The date beyond which the product should not be dispensed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A lot number identifies the production batch so affected stock can be traced during a recall, and the expiration date marks when the product should no longer be dispensed. Why the others are wrong: **C** patient information is not on the manufacturer's stock label; **D** a prescriber's DEA number is unrelated to lot/expiration data.

questions.stem: A pharmacy needs to document expired Schedule II controlled substances that it is destroying or sending to a reverse distributor. Which DEA form is used to record this disposal of controlled substances?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** DEA Form 41 is the Registrant Record of Controlled Substances Destroyed, used to document the disposal/destruction of controlled substances. Why the others are wrong: **A** Form 222 is for ordering Schedule II drugs; **B** Form 224 is the pharmacy's DEA registration application; **D** MedWatch 3500 reports adverse events, not controlled-substance disposal.

questions.stem: Under the federal Controlled Substances Act, which schedule contains drugs with no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Schedule I drugs (e.g., heroin, LSD) have a high abuse potential and no accepted medical use in the United States, so they are not dispensed in pharmacies. Why the others are wrong: **B** Schedule II drugs have accepted medical uses despite high abuse potential; **C** and **D** have progressively lower abuse potential and accepted medical uses.

questions.stem: A prescription for oxycodone (a Schedule II controlled substance) is presented. Which statement reflects federal requirements for CII prescriptions?

options.text: Refills are unlimited for one year
Up to five refills are allowed within six months
Refills are not permitted on a Schedule II prescription
One automatic refill is added by the pharmacy

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Federal law prohibits refills on Schedule II prescriptions; a new prescription is required each time. Why the others are wrong: **A** unlimited refills are never allowed for controlled substances; **B** the five-refills-in-six-months rule applies to Schedule III–V drugs, not CII; **D** pharmacies cannot add refills to a CII.

questions.stem: A prescription for a Schedule III–V controlled substance, if authorized by the prescriber, may be refilled a maximum of how many times and within what period under federal law?

options.text: Up to 5 refills within 6 months of the date written

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** For Schedule III–V drugs, federal law allows a maximum of five refills within six months of the issue date if authorized. Why the others are wrong: **A** refills are capped, never unlimited; **B** 11 refills/12 months applies to many non-controlled prescriptions, not CIII–V; **C** no refills is the rule for Schedule II.

questions.stem: DEA Form 222 (or its electronic CSOS equivalent) is required for which activity?

options.text: Reporting an adverse drug event to the FDA
Ordering Schedule II controlled substances from a supplier
Dispensing a Schedule IV prescription to a patient

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** DEA Form 222 (or the electronic CSOS system) is used to order or transfer Schedule II controlled substances between registrants. Why the others are wrong: **A** adverse events go through MedWatch; **C** dispensing a CIV prescription does not require Form 222; **D** returning OTC products is unrelated to the controlled-substance ordering form.

questions.stem: Isotretinoin can only be dispensed through the iPLEDGE program because of its risk of severe birth defects. iPLEDGE is an example of what kind of program?

options.text: A Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS)

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** iPLEDGE is a REMS, an FDA-required risk-management program with special requirements to ensure isotretinoin's benefits outweigh its serious teratogenic risk. Why the others are wrong: **A** a recall classification (Class I–III) rates a product defect's hazard; **B** a PDMP tracks controlled-substance dispensing; **D** a formulary tier is an insurance coverage level.

questions.stem: The FDA issues a recall for a drug because there is a reasonable probability that its use will cause serious adverse health consequences or death. This is which class of recall?
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A Class I recall is the most serious—use of the product carries a reasonable probability of serious harm or death. Why the others are wrong: **A** a market withdrawal involves a minor issue not subject to legal action; **B** Class II involves temporary or medically reversible harm; **C** Class III is unlikely to cause adverse health effects.

questions.stem: The Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA) was enacted primarily to:

options.text: Enable tracing of prescription drugs through the supply chain to keep counterfeit and harmful drugs out
Set the copay amounts patients pay at the pharmacy
Establish the schedules for controlled substances
Require child-resistant packaging on all medications

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** DSCSA builds an electronic, interoperable system to trace prescription drugs through the U.S. supply chain, helping keep counterfeit, stolen, or harmful products out. Why the others are wrong: **B** copays are set by insurers; **C** drug schedules come from the Controlled Substances Act; **D** child-resistant packaging is governed by the Poison Prevention Packaging Act.

questions.stem: Hazardous drugs such as certain chemotherapy agents must be handled per which USP chapter, which addresses receipt, storage, compounding, and disposal to protect personnel?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** USP <800> governs the safe handling of hazardous drugs—including receipt, storage, compounding, and disposal—to protect workers, patients, and the environment. Why the others are wrong: **A** USP <795> covers non-sterile compounding; **C** USP <797> covers sterile compounding; **D** USP <71> addresses sterility testing.

questions.stem: A prescription is written for Coumadin. Which generic anticoagulant is being dispensed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Coumadin is the brand name for warfarin, an oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant. Why the others are wrong: **A** clopidogrel is an antiplatelet sold as Plavix; **C** enoxaparin is a low-molecular-weight heparin marketed as Lovenox; **D** rivaroxaban is a direct oral anticoagulant sold as Xarelto.

questions.stem: Sertraline is best classified as which type of antidepressant?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Sertraline (Zoloft) is an SSRI that increases serotonin availability and is a first-line treatment for depression and anxiety. Why the others are wrong: **A** TCAs include amitriptyline and nortriptyline; **B** MAOIs include phenelzine and selegiline; **D** benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are sedative-anxiolytics, not antidepressants.

questions.stem: Losartan lowers blood pressure as a member of which drug class, identifiable by its -sartan stem?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Losartan (Cozaar) is an angiotensin II receptor blocker; the -sartan stem marks the ARB class. Why the others are wrong: **B** ACE inhibitors end in -pril; **C** beta blockers end in -olol; **D** thiazides such as hydrochlorothiazide are a separate diuretic class.

questions.stem: A patient picking up an oral tetracycline antibiotic such as doxycycline should receive which counseling point, reflecting a common interaction?

options.text: Take it together with milk or an antacid to improve absorption
Separate it from dairy products, antacids, and iron because they reduce its absorption
Double the dose if a meal is skipped
It has no clinically meaningful food or mineral interactions

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Polyvalent cations in dairy, antacids, and iron chelate tetracyclines and markedly reduce absorption, so these should be separated by a couple of hours. Why the others are wrong: **A** taking it with milk decreases, not increases, absorption; **C** patients should never double doses on their own; **D** the chelation interaction is clinically significant.

questions.stem: A transdermal fentanyl patch delivers medication by which route of administration?

options.text: Through the skin into the systemic circulation

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A transdermal patch releases drug across intact skin for absorption into the bloodstream, giving sustained systemic delivery. Why the others are wrong: **B** intramuscular delivery uses an injection into muscle; **C** inhalation delivers drug to the lungs; **D** the rectal route uses suppositories or enemas, none of which describe a skin patch.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin is counseled to keep their intake of which nutrient consistent because large changes can reduce the drug's effectiveness?

options.text: Vitamin K (found in leafy green vegetables)

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Warfarin works by antagonizing vitamin K, so sharp swings in dietary vitamin K (leafy greens) can blunt or exaggerate its effect; consistency is the key counseling point. Why the others are wrong: **A** vitamin C, **C** calcium, and **D** vitamin D do not directly oppose warfarin's anticoagulant mechanism.

questions.stem: An auxiliary label stating "Avoid prolonged exposure to sunlight" is most appropriate on a prescription for which medication?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Doxycycline and other tetracyclines cause photosensitivity, so a sun-exposure warning label is appropriate. Why the others are wrong: **A** calcium carbonate, **C** levothyroxine, and **D** docusate are not associated with photosensitivity and would not carry that auxiliary label.

questions.stem: A reconstituted vial of a biologic is labeled "protect from light; do not shake." The instruction not to shake is intended primarily to prevent:

options.text: Denaturation or aggregation of the protein, which can reduce potency
The solution from becoming too cold
A change in the product's color only, with no effect on potency
The vial label from peeling off

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Vigorous shaking introduces shear stress and foaming that can denature or aggregate protein-based drugs, degrading potency; gentle swirling is advised. Why the others are wrong: **B** shaking does not lower temperature; **C** the concern is loss of activity, not just appearance; **D** label adhesion is unrelated to the instruction.

questions.stem: Which two medications are correctly matched with the condition they are primarily used to treat? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Metformin is a first-line oral agent for type 2 diabetes and levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone in hypothyroidism. Why the others are wrong: **C** albuterol is a bronchodilator for asthma/COPD, not hypertension; **D** omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor for acid-related disorders, not an antibiotic.

questions.stem: A technician is matching generic drugs to their brand names. Which two pairs below are matched correctly? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Gabapentin is sold as Neurontin and sildenafil as Viagra; both pairings are correct. Why the others are wrong: **C** montelukast's brand is Singulair, whereas Zofran is ondansetron; **D** escitalopram is Lexapro, while Cymbalta is duloxetine.

questions.stem: Amlodipine is classified as which type of cardiovascular medication?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Amlodipine (Norvasc) is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, identifiable by the -dipine stem, used for hypertension and angina. Why the others are wrong: **A** ACE inhibitors end in -pril; **C** loop diuretics include furosemide; **D** statins end in -statin and lower cholesterol.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed prednisone and asks the technician about a common side effect of oral corticosteroids. Which effect is well established for this class?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone commonly raise blood glucose and can also cause fluid retention and increased appetite. Why the others are wrong: **B** tooth discoloration is linked to tetracyclines; **C** a dry cough is an ACE-inhibitor effect; **D** orange urine is associated with phenazopyridine.

questions.stem: A patient already taking sertraline is started on tramadol for pain. Why should the pharmacist be alerted to this combination?

options.text: The two drugs are chemically identical and the dose would be doubled
Both increase serotonin activity, raising the risk of serotonin syndrome
Tramadol blocks the absorption of sertraline in the stomach
The combination is preferred and requires no review

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Sertraline (an SSRI) and tramadol both raise serotonin levels, so combining them increases the risk of serotonin syndrome, a serious interaction warranting pharmacist review. Why the others are wrong: **A** the drugs are different agents; **C** the concern is additive serotonergic effect, not absorption; **D** the interaction is potentially harmful, so review is needed.

questions.stem: Writing a dose as "0.5 mg" instead of ".5 mg" is an error-prevention practice known as using a:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A leading zero before a decimal point (0.5 mg) ensures the decimal is seen, preventing a tenfold overdose from a misread ".5 mg." Why the others are wrong: **A** a trailing zero (5.0 mg) is prohibited because it can be misread as 50; **C** Tall Man lettering distinguishes similar drug names; **D** bar codes verify products electronically.

questions.stem: The error-prone abbreviation "U" for units appears on the ISMP "Do Not Use" list because it can be misread as:

options.text: The number 0 or 4, leading to overdose

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A handwritten "U" can be mistaken for a 0 or 4 (e.g., 4U read as 40 or 44), causing a major insulin overdose, so "unit" should be spelled out. Why the others are wrong: **B** "daily" relates to the abbreviation QD; **C** the microgram confusion involves µg vs mg; **D** "U" is not a route abbreviation.

questions.stem: Concentrated potassium chloride for injection is treated as a high-alert medication primarily because:

options.text: It is very expensive to replace
Inadvertent IV administration of the concentrate can be rapidly fatal

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Undiluted concentrated potassium chloride given IV can cause fatal cardiac arrest, which is why it is a classic high-alert drug removed from floor stock. Why the others are wrong: **A** cost does not define high-alert status; **C** it does not stain skin; **D** refrigeration is unrelated to its high-alert designation.

questions.stem: A technician notices an error reached a patient but caused no harm, while a separate mistake was caught before reaching the patient. The mistake caught beforehand is best described as a:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A near miss is an error that is intercepted before it reaches the patient; reporting it helps prevent future harm. Why the others are wrong: **A** a sentinel event is an unexpected event causing serious harm or death; **C** an adverse drug event involves actual patient harm from a drug; **D** a Class I recall concerns a defective product, not a dispensing slip.

questions.stem: During order entry a technician sees that a prescribed dose appears far higher than usual for the drug. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Adjust the dose to a normal amount and continue filling
Refer the order to the pharmacist to evaluate the dose
Call the patient and tell them not to take the medication
Cancel the prescription without notifying anyone

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Judging whether an unusually high dose is appropriate is a clinical decision, so the technician must refer it to the pharmacist. Why the others are wrong: **A** changing a dose is outside the technician's scope; **C** advising a patient about therapy is the pharmacist's role; **D** silently canceling a valid order is inappropriate.

questions.stem: A horizontal laminar airflow workbench used for non-hazardous sterile compounding directs filtered air:

options.text: From the HEPA filter at the back, horizontally toward the compounder
Downward from the ceiling onto the work surface
From the compounder's body toward the product
Randomly in all directions to maximize coverage

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** In a horizontal laminar airflow hood, HEPA-filtered air flows from the back of the cabinet horizontally across the work surface toward the operator, keeping the critical site sterile. Why the others are wrong: **B** describes vertical airflow; **C** would carry contaminants from the worker onto the product; **D** laminar means unidirectional, not random, airflow.

questions.stem: When compounding hazardous drugs such as chemotherapy, the recommended primary engineering control is a:

options.text: Biological safety cabinet (or compounding aseptic containment isolator) that protects both product and worker
An open countertop near a window

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Hazardous-drug compounding requires a containment primary engineering control such as a Class II biological safety cabinet or CACI, which protects the preparation and the worker via negative pressure and external venting. Why the others are wrong: **A** a horizontal hood blows air toward the worker, exposing them to the drug; **C** an open counter offers no containment; **D** a refrigerator is for storage, not compounding.

questions.stem: Which two strategies specifically help prevent errors with high-alert medications? (Select two.)

options.text: Requiring an independent double-check by a second person
Standardizing concentrations and limiting available strengths
Storing them loose alongside all other floor-stock drugs
Removing bar-code verification to save time

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Independent double-checks and standardizing/limiting concentrations are recognized safeguards that reduce harm from high-alert drugs. Why the others are wrong: **C** these drugs should be sequestered, not mixed loosely with general stock; **D** bar-code verification is a safety control that should be kept, not removed.

questions.stem: Which pair is a classic look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) combination addressed with Tall Man lettering?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Dopamine and dobutamine are a well-known LASA pair distinguished by Tall Man lettering as DOPamine and DOBUTamine. Why the others are wrong: **A** aspirin and acetaminophen have distinct names; **C** sodium and potassium are different electrolytes, not a name look-alike pair; **D** ibuprofen and naproxen are both NSAIDs but their names are not confusable.

questions.stem: Bar-code scanning of a product's NDC during the fill process primarily helps to:

options.text: Confirm the correct drug and strength were selected, reducing wrong-drug errors
Print the pharmacy's hours on the label
Replace the pharmacist's final verification entirely

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Scanning the product bar code matches the NDC to the order, catching wrong-drug or wrong-strength selections before dispensing. Why the others are wrong: **B** copays come from the insurance adjudication, not the bar code; **C** store hours are not derived from scanning; **D** bar coding supports but does not replace the pharmacist's clinical check.

questions.stem: The Sig "1 gtt OU bid" instructs the patient to administer:

options.text: 1 drop in the left eye twice daily
1 drop in both eyes twice daily
1 drop in both ears twice daily

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** "gtt" means drop, "OU" means both eyes, and "bid" means twice daily, so the directions are 1 drop in both eyes twice daily. Why the others are wrong: **A** the left eye is OS; **C** there is no tablet ("gtt" is drops); **D** both ears would be AU, not OU.

questions.stem: A child weighing 22 kg is prescribed a drug at 10 mg/kg/day divided into two equal doses. How many milligrams are in each dose?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** 10 mg/kg × 22 kg = 220 mg/day; divided into two doses gives 110 mg per dose. Why the others are wrong: **A** 220 mg is the full daily dose, not a single dose; **C** 44 mg ignores the mg/kg rate; **D** 20 mg has no basis in the calculation.

questions.stem: How many grams of hydrocortisone are needed to compound 60 g of a 2.5% (w/w) hydrocortisone ointment?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** 2.5% w/w means 2.5 g per 100 g, so 60 g × 0.025 = 1.5 g of hydrocortisone. Why the others are wrong: **A** 0.15 g is off by a factor of ten; **C** 15 g would be a 25% preparation; **D** 2.5 g is the amount in 100 g, not 60 g.

questions.stem: A medication order reads 1.5 g. How many milligrams is this?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** There are 1000 mg in 1 g, so 1.5 g × 1000 = 1500 mg. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **B** move the decimal the wrong number of places; **D** converts in the wrong direction, treating grams as a smaller unit than milligrams.

questions.stem: An insulin order calls for 40 units of U-100 insulin to be drawn up. What volume should be withdrawn?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** U-100 insulin contains 100 units/mL, so 40 units ÷ 100 units/mL = 0.4 mL. Why the others are wrong: **B** 4 mL would be 400 units; **C** 0.04 mL is off by a factor of ten; **D** 40 mL would be 4000 units, a massive overdose.

questions.stem: Which piece of equipment is most appropriate for accurately measuring a small liquid volume such as 3.5 mL when compounding?

options.text: An oral syringe or appropriately sized graduate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A syringe or a suitably small graduated cylinder gives accurate measurement of small liquid volumes. Why the others are wrong: **B** a balance weighs solids, not liquid volume; **C** a mortar and pestle grind or mix, they do not measure volume; **D** a counting tray is used to count solid tablets and capsules.

questions.stem: When pulling stock for returns, a technician finds a multi-dose vial with a manufacturer expiration of 12/2026 but no beyond-use date written after opening. The technician should:

options.text: Assume it is usable until 12/2026 regardless of when it was opened
Recognize that once opened the beyond-use date may be shorter than the labeled expiration and refer to policy
Re-label it with a new manufacturer expiration date

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** After a multi-dose vial is opened, its beyond-use date is often shorter (commonly 28 days) than the printed expiration, so the technician follows facility policy on opened-vial BUDs. Why the others are wrong: **A** the manufacturer date applies only to the unopened product; **C** unopened, in-date stock should not be discarded wholesale; **D** technicians cannot fabricate a new manufacturer expiration date.

questions.stem: Which two practices support proper management of expired or non-dispensable stock? (Select two.)

options.text: Rotating stock so shorter-dated product is used first (FEFO)
Quarantining expired or recalled product away from active dispensing stock
Returning expired controlled substances to active inventory
Leaving recalled lots on the shelf until they are dispensed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** First-expired-first-out rotation and quarantining expired or recalled product both prevent dispensing of unusable stock. Why the others are wrong: **C** expired controlled substances must be removed and documented for disposal, not returned to inventory; **D** recalled lots must be pulled and segregated, never left to be dispensed.

questions.stem: Place the following metric weights in order from smallest to largest mass.
questions.explanation: Each metric unit is 1000 times the one before it, so from smallest to largest the order is microgram, milligram, gram, kilogram. One microgram (A) is the smallest; 1000 micrograms make a milligram (B); 1000 milligrams make a gram (C); and 1000 grams make a kilogram (D), the largest. Knowing these 1000-fold steps lets a technician convert reliably and catch decimal errors.

questions.stem: Alprazolam (Xanax), a commonly prescribed benzodiazepine, is classified under which federal controlled-substance schedule?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam, lorazepam, and diazepam are Schedule IV controlled substances. Why the others are wrong: **A** Schedule II includes drugs like oxycodone and fentanyl; **B** Schedule III includes products such as certain codeine combinations and ketamine; **D** Schedule V includes low-dose codeine cough preparations.

questions.stem: A prescriber's DEA registration number for "Dr. Adams" begins AA and is followed by 1234562. To validate the number, you add the 1st, 3rd, and 5th digits and the 2nd, 4th, and 6th digits, multiply the second sum by 2, and add the two results; the last digit of that total should equal the number's:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In the DEA-number checksum, (digits 1+3+5) + 2×(digits 2+4+6) yields a number whose last digit must match the 7th digit (the check digit). For 1234562: (1+3+5)=9 and 2×(2+4+6)=24, totaling 33, whose last digit 3 should match digit 7—but here it is 2, so the number is invalid. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **C** the letters identify the registrant type and last name, not the checksum result; **D** the ZIP code is not encoded in a DEA number.

questions.stem: A patient wants to return unused Schedule II tablets for safe disposal. Which option is consistent with DEA rules for patient drug disposal?

options.text: The pharmacy technician personally takes them back over the counter and restocks them
Directing the patient to an authorized take-back program or collection receptacle
Telling the patient pharmacies may always accept any returned controlled substance
Refilling the leftover tablets into a new patient's prescription

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** DEA disposal rules let patients surrender controlled substances through authorized take-back events or collection receptacles. Why the others are wrong: **A** dispensed controlled substances cannot be taken back and restocked; **C** pharmacies may only collect if they are authorized collectors, so "always" is incorrect; **D** reusing a patient's medication for someone else is illegal and unsafe.

questions.stem: Clozapine carries a boxed warning for severe neutropenia; its labeling requires monitoring of which laboratory value before dispensing?

options.text: Absolute neutrophil count (ANC), due to the risk of severe neutropenia
Blood glucose, due to the risk of diabetes
Serum sodium, due to the risk of dehydration

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Clozapine's labeling requires absolute neutrophil count (ANC) monitoring because the drug can cause severe neutropenia (agranulocytosis); an adequate ANC is needed before dispensing. (The FDA-required clozapine REMS was discontinued in 2025, but ANC monitoring under the prescribing information continues.) Why the others are wrong: **B**, **C**, and **D** are general health parameters but are not the specific lab tied to clozapine's neutropenia risk.

questions.stem: Under federal law, how long must a pharmacy generally retain controlled-substance records to be available for DEA inspection?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Federal law requires controlled-substance records to be kept for a minimum of two years (some states require longer). Why the others are wrong: **B** 30 days is far too short and not a federal record-keeping standard; **C** 10 years exceeds the federal minimum; **D** retention of these records is mandatory, not optional.

questions.stem: Under the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (CMEA), nonprescription products containing pseudoephedrine must be:

options.text: Sold freely on open shelves with no limits
Kept behind the counter with purchase-quantity limits and a logbook of buyer information
Dispensed only on a Schedule II prescription

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The CMEA requires pseudoephedrine to be stored behind the counter, with daily/monthly purchase limits and a logbook capturing the buyer's identification. Why the others are wrong: **A** open-shelf sales are exactly what the law restricts; **C** pseudoephedrine remains nonprescription federally, not a CII drug; **D** Form 222 is for ordering Schedule II substances, not pseudoephedrine controls.

questions.stem: Under the DSCSA, which two pieces of documentation must accompany prescription drug products as they move through the supply chain to authorized trading partners? (Select two.)

options.text: Transaction Information (TI) describing the product and the transaction
A Transaction Statement (TS) affirming compliant handling of the product
A copy of the pharmacist's personal license posted on the box

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** DSCSA requires Transaction Information and a Transaction Statement (historically also Transaction History) to follow products between trading partners to support tracing. Why the others are wrong: **C** patient insurance information is unrelated to supply-chain tracing; **D** the supply-chain documents are about the product's chain of custody, not an individual's license affixed to a carton.

questions.stem: Non-sterile compounding, such as preparing an ointment or an oral suspension from bulk ingredients, is governed by which USP chapter?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** USP <795> sets the standards for non-sterile compounding, including ointments, capsules, and oral liquids. Why the others are wrong: **B** USP <797> governs sterile compounding; **C** USP <800> covers handling of hazardous drugs; **D** combines the sterile and hazardous chapters, neither of which is the non-sterile standard.

questions.stem: A prescription is written for Synthroid. Which generic drug should be dispensed?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Synthroid is the brand name for levothyroxine, a synthetic T4 thyroid hormone used to treat hypothyroidism. Why the others are wrong: **A** liothyronine is synthetic T3 (Cytomel), a different thyroid product; **C** methimazole (Tapazole) is an antithyroid drug used for hyperthyroidism, the opposite indication; **D** metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic, not a thyroid agent.

questions.stem: Ciprofloxacin belongs to which class of antibiotics, identifiable by the -floxacin stem?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone, recognizable by the -floxacin stem, that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase. Why the others are wrong: **A** cephalosporins typically start with cef-/ceph- (cephalexin); **B** aminoglycosides end in -micin/-mycin (gentamicin); **D** sulfonamides include sulfamethoxazole and are a distinct class.

questions.stem: A patient taking allopurinol for gout is started on azathioprine. Why is this combination flagged for the pharmacist?

options.text: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which can raise azathioprine levels and toxicity
The two drugs are identical and the dose would simply double
Allopurinol blocks azathioprine from being absorbed in the gut
There is no interaction and the combination is always preferred

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks down azathioprine's active metabolite, so co-administration can cause dangerous accumulation and bone-marrow toxicity unless doses are reduced. Why the others are wrong: **B** the drugs are different agents in different classes; **C** the mechanism is impaired metabolism, not blocked absorption; **D** this is a clinically significant interaction requiring review.

questions.stem: An enteric-coated tablet is designed with a special coating primarily to:

options.text: Dissolve rapidly in the mouth before swallowing
Resist stomach acid and dissolve in the intestine, protecting the stomach or the drug
Allow the tablet to be safely crushed and given in food
Make the tablet float on top of stomach contents

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An enteric coating resists gastric acid so the tablet passes intact into the more alkaline intestine before dissolving, which protects an acid-sensitive drug or shields the stomach from irritation. Why the others are wrong: **A** describes an orally disintegrating tablet; **C** enteric-coated tablets generally must not be crushed, which would defeat the coating; **D** floating delivery is a separate gastroretentive design.

questions.stem: Ondansetron (Zofran) is primarily indicated for which purpose?

options.text: Preventing and treating nausea and vomiting

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist (antiemetic) used to prevent and treat nausea and vomiting, including chemotherapy- and surgery-related nausea. Why the others are wrong: **A** blood pressure is managed by agents like ACE inhibitors; **C** ondansetron is not an antibiotic; **D** decongestants such as pseudoephedrine relieve congestion.

questions.stem: A nitroglycerin sublingual tablet's original glass container carries the instruction to keep it tightly closed because the drug is sensitive to:

options.text: Light, heat, air, and moisture, which cause loss of potency

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Sublingual nitroglycerin is volatile and unstable, so it is kept in its original tightly closed glass container away from light, heat, air, and moisture to preserve potency. Why the others are wrong: **A** cold is not the primary concern; **C** scanning does not affect drug stability; **D** orientation of the bottle does not determine potency loss.

questions.stem: Hydrocodone/acetaminophen is commonly dispensed under which brand name?
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Norco is a brand combining hydrocodone with acetaminophen. Why the others are wrong: **B** Percocet is oxycodone with acetaminophen; **C** Ultram is tramadol; **D** Dilaudid is hydromorphone. Each is a different opioid product.

questions.stem: Which counseling point is most appropriate for a patient starting an oral bisphosphonate such as alendronate (Fosamax)?

options.text: Take it at bedtime with a large meal
Take it on an empty stomach with a full glass of water and remain upright for at least 30 minutes
Take it with an antacid to reduce stomach upset
Lie down immediately after taking it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Oral bisphosphonates are taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, and the patient stays upright for at least 30 minutes to maximize absorption and prevent esophageal irritation. Why the others are wrong: **A** food and minerals drastically reduce absorption; **C** antacids contain cations that bind the drug and impair absorption; **D** lying down increases the risk of esophageal injury.

questions.stem: Metronidazole (Flagyl) most often carries an auxiliary label warning patients to:

options.text: Avoid alcohol because of a possible disulfiram-like reaction
Take it only on a completely full bladder
Expect the medication to cause hair loss

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Metronidazole can cause a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, nausea, vomiting) when combined with alcohol, so patients are warned to avoid alcohol during and shortly after therapy. Why the others are wrong: **B** dairy is not the key concern for metronidazole; **C** bladder status is irrelevant to dosing; **D** hair loss is not a characteristic metronidazole effect.

questions.stem: A patient on lisinopril is started on potassium-sparing spironolactone and a potassium supplement. Why should the pharmacist review this regimen?

options.text: It guarantees the blood pressure will drop too low every time
The combination raises the risk of hyperkalemia (dangerously high potassium)
The three agents must always be taken together for safety

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, and potassium supplements each raise serum potassium, so combining them increases the risk of hyperkalemia, which can cause serious cardiac arrhythmias. Why the others are wrong: **A** hypotension is possible but not guaranteed and is not the primary additive risk here; **C** spironolactone does not nullify lisinopril; **D** these are not required to be combined and doing so without monitoring is the concern.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are correctly paired with the drug class identified by their name stem? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Pantoprazole's -prazole stem marks it as a proton pump inhibitor, and cephalexin's ceph- prefix identifies a cephalosporin antibiotic. Why the others are wrong: **B** clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist, not a benzodiazepine, and lacks the -pam stem; **D** atenolol ends in -olol and is a beta blocker, not a calcium channel blocker.

questions.stem: Which two medications should typically be protected from light during storage to preserve their stability? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Nitroprusside and phytonadione (vitamin K) are both light-sensitive and are protected from light (e.g., wrapped or amber-covered) to prevent degradation. Why the others are wrong: **C** 0.9% sodium chloride and **D** sterile water for irrigation are stable, non-light-sensitive solutions that do not require light protection.

questions.stem: Furosemide (Lasix) belongs to which class of diuretics?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Furosemide is a loop diuretic that acts on the loop of Henle and is widely used for edema and heart failure. Why the others are wrong: **A** spironolactone and triamterene are potassium-sparing diuretics; **B** hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide; **D** mannitol is an osmotic diuretic.

questions.stem: Heparin is treated as a high-alert medication primarily because:

options.text: It frequently causes permanent skin discoloration
Dosing errors can lead to serious bleeding or thrombosis
It must be reconstituted before every use
It is the most expensive injectable in the pharmacy

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Heparin is an anticoagulant whose dosing errors can cause life-threatening bleeding or, if underdosed, clot formation, which is why it is a classic high-alert drug. Why the others are wrong: **A** skin discoloration is not the basis for its designation; **C** many heparin products are ready-to-use, and reconstitution is not why it is high-alert; **D** cost does not determine high-alert status.

questions.stem: Predni​SONE and predniSOLONE are differentiated with Tall Man lettering because they are:

options.text: A look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) pair that can be confused
Identical drugs with the same strengths
Two different routes of the same injection

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** PredniSONE and predniSOLONE have very similar spelling and sound, making them a LASA pair that Tall Man lettering helps distinguish. Why the others are wrong: **B** these corticosteroids are not controlled substances; **C** they are related but distinct drugs, not identical; **D** they are separate oral corticosteroids, not two routes of one injection.

questions.stem: A patient asks the pharmacy technician which over-the-counter product would be best for a new, worsening symptom. The technician should:

options.text: Recommend the product they personally prefer
Refer the patient to the pharmacist for the recommendation
Tell the patient any product on the shelf will work
Advise the patient to take a prescription-strength dose

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Recommending a therapy and assessing symptoms involve clinical judgment reserved for the pharmacist, so the technician refers the patient. Why the others are wrong: **A** a technician should not make a clinical product recommendation; **C** dismissively saying any product works is inaccurate and unsafe; **D** advising prescription-strength dosing is outside the technician's scope.

questions.stem: An unexpected occurrence involving death or serious physical or psychological injury, signaling the need for immediate investigation, is known by The Joint Commission as a:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A sentinel event is a patient-safety event resulting in death or serious harm that signals the need for immediate investigation and response. Why the others are wrong: **A** a near miss is intercepted before reaching the patient and causes no harm; **C** an omission error is a missed dose, not necessarily serious harm; **D** a Class III recall concerns a low-risk product defect, not a patient-safety event.

questions.stem: How often should the certification of a laminar airflow primary engineering control used for sterile compounding generally be performed to confirm it still meets standards?

options.text: Only once when it is first installed
At least every 6 months (and after relocation or major service)
Never, as long as it powers on

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Primary engineering controls such as laminar airflow hoods are recertified at least every 6 months, and also after they are moved or undergo major service, to verify airflow and filter integrity. Why the others are wrong: **A** a single installation check is insufficient for ongoing assurance; **C** a 10-year interval is far too long; **D** simply powering on does not confirm the unit meets air-cleanliness standards.

questions.stem: Within an ISO-classified cleanroom for sterile compounding, which area must maintain the cleanest air quality (ISO Class 5)?

options.text: The direct compounding area inside the primary engineering control

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The direct compounding area within the primary engineering control (e.g., the laminar airflow hood) must maintain ISO Class 5 air, the cleanest classification, because that is where critical sites are exposed. Why the others are wrong: **A** the ante-area is a lower classification used for garbing and staging; **C** a hallway and **D** a break room are unclassified, far dirtier spaces.

questions.stem: Why is the abbreviation "IU" (for international units) on the ISMP list of error-prone abbreviations?

options.text: It can be misread as 'IV' (intravenous) or the number 10
It always means the same as milligrams
It is only used for topical products

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Handwritten "IU" can be mistaken for "IV" or the number 10, so "international units" should be written out. Why the others are wrong: **B** international units are an activity-based measure, not equivalent to milligrams; **C** IU is not limited to topicals; **D** "immediately" is conveyed by "stat," not IU.

questions.stem: Which two abbreviations appear on the ISMP/Joint Commission "Do Not Use" list and should be spelled out instead? (Select two.)
questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** "QD" can be misread as QID or OD, and "MS/MSO4" is ambiguous between morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate, so both should be written out. Why the others are wrong: **C** "mL" is an accepted standard unit abbreviation; **D** "mg" is likewise accepted and not on the do-not-use list.

questions.stem: After removing single-use gloves following a compounding task, the most important next step for infection prevention is to:

options.text: Reuse the gloves for the next patient's preparation
Place the gloves back in the box

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Hands can become contaminated during glove removal, so performing hand hygiene immediately afterward is the key infection-prevention step. Why the others are wrong: **A** single-use gloves are never reused; **C** touching surfaces before hand hygiene spreads contamination; **D** used gloves are discarded, not returned to the box.

questions.stem: A repeated pattern of the same dispensing error prompts the pharmacy to track data over time and test small process changes to reduce it. This ongoing approach is best described as:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Continuous quality improvement is an ongoing, data-driven process of measuring outcomes and testing changes to steadily reduce errors. Why the others are wrong: **B** a market withdrawal removes a product, not a process problem; **C** a formulary addition concerns which drugs are stocked; **D** inventory turnover is a stock-management metric, not an error-reduction method.

questions.stem: The Sig "ii tabs po q6h prn" directs the patient to take:

options.text: 2 tablets by mouth every 6 hours as needed
2 tablets by mouth every 6 days as needed
1 tablet under the tongue every 6 hours

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** "ii" is the Roman numeral 2, "tabs" is tablets, "po" is by mouth, "q6h" is every 6 hours, and "prn" is as needed. Why the others are wrong: **B** q6h is every 6 hours, not days; **C** there is no sublingual or single-tablet instruction; **D** po means by mouth, not rectally, and prn means as needed rather than routine.

questions.stem: A 2 L bag of normal saline is ordered to infuse at 125 mL/hr. Approximately how many hours will the infusion last?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** 2 L equals 2000 mL, and 2000 mL ÷ 125 mL/hr = 16 hours. Why the others are wrong: **A** 8 hours assumes 250 mL/hr; **B** 12 hours has no basis in the numbers; **D** 24 hours would require a rate of about 83 mL/hr.

questions.stem: A prescriber orders 2 teaspoonfuls of a liquid per dose. How many milliliters should the patient measure per dose?
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** One teaspoonful is standardized as 5 mL, so 2 teaspoonfuls = 10 mL. Why the others are wrong: **A** 5 mL is a single teaspoonful; **C** 15 mL equals one tablespoonful (3 teaspoonfuls); **D** 30 mL equals one fluid ounce.

questions.stem: A pharmacy stocks a 250 mg/5 mL amoxicillin suspension. A prescription calls for 400 mg per dose. What volume delivers one dose?
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The concentration is 250 mg/5 mL = 50 mg/mL, so 400 mg ÷ 50 mg/mL = 8 mL per dose. Why the others are wrong: **A** 4 mL gives 200 mg; **B** 6 mL gives 300 mg; **D** 10 mL gives 500 mg.

questions.stem: When using a Class A prescription balance, the smallest quantity that can be weighed within an acceptable 5% error (the minimum weighable quantity) is typically:

options.text: About 120 mg, based on a 6 mg sensitivity requirement
Exactly 1 g regardless of the balance
Any amount, because the balance has no lower limit

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** With a typical sensitivity requirement of 6 mg and a 5% acceptable error, the minimum weighable quantity is 6 mg ÷ 0.05 = 120 mg. Why the others are wrong: **B** the minimum depends on sensitivity, not a flat 1 g; **C** weighing below the minimum exceeds acceptable error; **D** 1 mg is far below the reliable range of a Class A balance.

questions.stem: On an 11-digit NDC formatted 5-4-2, the final two digits identify:

options.text: The drug's strength and dosage form

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** In the three-segment NDC, the last segment (here two digits) designates the package size and type. Why the others are wrong: **A** the first segment is the labeler/manufacturer; **B** the middle segment encodes strength, dosage form, and formulation; **D** prescriber information is never part of the NDC.

questions.stem: Which two pieces of equipment are appropriate for preparing a compounded ointment from bulk ingredients? (Select two.)

options.text: An ointment slab (or ointment pad) and spatula for levigation and mixing
A mortar and pestle for trituration
A laminar airflow hood used only for IV admixtures

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** An ointment slab with a spatula and a mortar and pestle are standard tools for levigating, triturating, and blending ingredients into a uniform non-sterile ointment. Why the others are wrong: **C** a laminar airflow hood is for sterile IV preparation, not a topical ointment; **D** a drop-counter is irrelevant to compounding a semisolid ointment.

questions.stem: Place the following liquid volumes in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: From smallest to largest the liquid measures are teaspoonful, tablespoonful, fluid ounce, then pint. One teaspoonful is 5 mL (A), the smallest; one tablespoonful equals three teaspoonfuls at 15 mL (B); one fluid ounce is 30 mL, or two tablespoonfuls (C); and one pint is 480 mL (D), by far the largest. Knowing these household-to-metric equivalents lets a technician convert dosing instructions accurately and choose the right measuring device.

questions.stem: Best practice for stock rotation in the pharmacy follows the FEFO principle, which means:

options.text: First-Expired, First-Out: dispense the shortest-dated stock first
Fastest-Earning, First-Out: sell the most profitable items first
Final-Entry, First-Out: dispense the most recently received stock first
Fewest-Errors, First-Out: pull whichever bottle is closest

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** FEFO stands for First-Expired, First-Out, meaning product with the nearest expiration date is dispensed first to minimize waste from expired stock. Why the others are wrong: **B** and **D** are not real inventory principles; **C** dispensing the newest stock first (LIFO) would let older product expire on the shelf.

questions.stem: Under federal law, a prescriber may authorize an emergency oral (verbal) prescription for a Schedule II drug, but a written, signed prescription must be provided to the pharmacy within:
questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** In a genuine emergency a CII may be dispensed on an oral order, but federal law requires the prescriber to deliver a signed written prescription to the pharmacy within 7 days. Why the others are wrong: **A** and **C** are shorter than the federal requirement; **D** 30 days far exceeds the allowed window.

questions.stem: Codeine-containing cough syrups with a low codeine content that may, where state law permits, be sold without a prescription are classified federally as:
questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Low-dose codeine cough preparations are Schedule V, the lowest-abuse-potential schedule, and federal law permits limited nonprescription sale where state law allows, with recordkeeping. Why the others are wrong: **A** Schedule II is high-abuse drugs like oxycodone; **B** Schedule III includes products like certain testosterone and ketamine; **C** Schedule IV includes benzodiazepines.

questions.stem: When a pharmacy returns Schedule II controlled substances to its supplier or a reverse distributor, which DEA form documents the transfer?

options.text: DEA Form 222 (or the CSOS electronic equivalent)

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A DEA Form 222 (or its CSOS electronic equivalent) is required to transfer Schedule II substances between registrants, including a pharmacy returning CII stock to a supplier or reverse distributor. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 41 documents destruction of controlled substances, not transfer; **C** Form 224 is the pharmacy's registration application; **D** Form 3500 is the FDA MedWatch adverse-event report.

questions.stem: Thalidomide and lenalidomide are dispensed only through a REMS with elements to assure safe use primarily because they carry a serious risk of:
questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Thalidomide and lenalidomide are potent teratogens, so their REMS requires controlled distribution and pregnancy prevention measures to avoid severe birth defects. Why the others are wrong: **B** hearing loss is associated with drugs like aminoglycosides; **C** tooth discoloration is linked to tetracyclines; **D** orange body fluids are associated with rifampin.

questions.stem: Under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act, most oral prescription drugs must be dispensed in child-resistant containers UNLESS:

options.text: The prescriber or the patient requests non-child-resistant packaging
The pharmacy is busy that day
The medication is a tablet rather than a capsule

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The Poison Prevention Packaging Act requires child-resistant containers but allows an exception when the prescriber or the patient requests easy-open (non-child-resistant) packaging. Why the others are wrong: **A** price does not affect the packaging requirement; **C** workload is not a legal exception; **D** the dosage form (tablet vs. capsule) is irrelevant to the requirement.

questions.stem: Under the DSCSA, when a pharmacy receives prescription drug stock, a core requirement is to verify that the product comes from an:

options.text: Authorized trading partner and is accompanied by required transaction documentation
Any source as long as the price is lowest

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** DSCSA requires trading partners to be authorized (appropriately licensed/registered) and product to arrive with the required transaction information and statement, supporting traceability and keeping illegitimate drugs out. Why the others are wrong: **B** missing documentation violates DSCSA tracing requirements; **C** anonymous marketplaces are not authorized trading partners; **D** price does not exempt a buyer from verification duties.

questions.stem: Which two requirements apply when handling hazardous drugs under USP <800>? (Select two.)

options.text: Storing hazardous drugs in a negative-pressure room, separated from non-hazardous inventory
Using appropriate PPE such as chemotherapy-tested gloves and a protective gown
Storing them on open shelves next to oral over-the-counter products
Disposing of hazardous waste in the regular pharmacy trash

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** USP <800> requires hazardous drugs to be stored in a negative-pressure, externally vented area separated from other stock, and personnel to wear suitable PPE such as chemo-tested gloves and gowns. Why the others are wrong: **C** open-shelf storage beside OTC products provides no containment; **D** hazardous waste must go into designated hazardous-waste streams, not regular trash.

questions.stem: An FDA recall in which a manufacturer voluntarily removes a product that is unlikely to cause adverse health consequences (for example, a minor labeling defect) is classified as a:
questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A Class III recall is the least serious category, used when exposure to the product is unlikely to cause adverse health effects, such as a minor labeling or container defect. Why the others are wrong: **A** Class I involves a reasonable probability of serious harm or death; **B** Class II involves temporary or reversible harm; **D** "sentinel recall" is not an FDA recall classification.

flashcards.back: Five federal schedules ranked by abuse potential. CI: no accepted medical use, high abuse (heroin, LSD). CII: high abuse, accepted use (oxycodone, fentanyl). CIII–CV: progressively lower abuse potential (e.g., CIII codeine combos, CIV alprazolam/lorazepam, CV low-dose codeine cough syrups).
Schedule II: no refills—a new prescription is required each time. Schedule III–V: up to 5 refills within 6 months of the date written, if authorized by the prescriber.
The form (or its electronic CSOS equivalent) required to order or transfer Schedule II controlled substances between DEA registrants. CIII–CV ordering does not require Form 222.

USP <795> = non-sterile compounding standards. USP <797> = sterile compounding (preventing microbial contamination). USP <800> = safe handling of hazardous drugs (e.g., chemotherapy) to protect personnel and the environment.

An FDA-required safety program for drugs with serious risks, adding requirements beyond normal labeling to ensure benefits outweigh risks. Examples: iPLEDGE for isotretinoin, and clozapine monitoring for severe neutropenia.
Class I: reasonable probability of serious harm or death (most serious). Class II: temporary or medically reversible harm. Class III: unlikely to cause adverse health effects (least serious).
A 10- or 11-digit code in three segments: (1) labeler/manufacturer, (2) product—strength, dosage form, and formulation, and (3) package size and type.
po = by mouth; bid = twice daily; tid = three times daily; qid = four times daily; qhs/hs = at bedtime; prn = as needed; gtt = drops; ac = before meals; pc = after meals; SL = sublingual.

A method to combine a higher- and lower-strength product to reach a desired in-between strength. Parts of the high strength = (desired − low); parts of the low strength = (high − desired). The 'tic-tac-toe' grid gives the proportion of each.
Expresses grams of solute per mL of solution: 1:1000 = 1 g in 1000 mL = 1 mg/mL. 1:100 = 1 g in 100 mL = 10 mg/mL. The larger the second number, the more dilute the solution.

An error-prevention strategy that uses mixed-case letters to emphasize the differing portions of look-alike/sound-alike (LASA) drug names—e.g., hydrOXYzine vs. hydrALAZINE, predniSONE vs. prednisoLONE.

Drugs that carry a heightened risk of significant harm when used in error. Classic examples (per ISMP): insulin, heparin/anticoagulants, opioids, concentrated electrolytes (e.g., potassium chloride), and chemotherapy. They warrant extra safeguards like independent double-checks.

-statin = HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (atorvastatin); -pril = ACE inhibitor (lisinopril); -olol = beta blocker (metoprolol); -sartan = ARB (losartan); -prazole = proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole); -dipine = calcium channel blocker (amlodipine).

Common items requiring refrigeration include insulin (unopened), many reconstituted antibiotic suspensions (e.g., amoxicillin), some injectables and vaccines, and certain eye drops/biologics. Insulin must never be frozen.
